content:
Earlier this year, Apple caught the entire PC market off guard with the launch of the MacBook Neo laptop. Although the aggressive pricing strategy of the device has had to be adjusted in response to market conditions, it has taken several months for Windows camp competitors to gradually unveil their own counter-offers. Now it's HP's turn — they have launched a brand-new laptop with an OLED display, starting at the same US$699 price point, but it comes with quite a few caveats.

Top comment posted by TurboFool

There's been a lot of Windows news around here lately that has no substantive connection to Google at all, and the situation is worrying. Some of it can be loosely considered related — for instance, at least being ARM devices, or having some tenuous connection to Android devices — but even that argument is quite a stretch. Now this is an x86 Windows laptop, and there is absolutely no reasonable justification for this news item to appear here. This situation concerns me greatly, because I migrated over from AP, AA and other sites, all of which gradually deteriorated, padding article counts with off-topic junk content. I really don't want to lose yet another one.

The HP OmniBook 5 14 looks essentially like a low-priced, eye-catching version of the MacBook Neo's chassis, paired with a hybrid of the more refined, understated green and blue tones of the Apple iPad Air lineup. At 11.77mm thick and weighing just 2.56 pounds despite its 14-inch display, it seems perfectly timed for the back-to-school shopping season — except HP has pretty much missed that window. The real star of the show, however, is that 14-inch display, which swaps out the IPS panels commonly found at this price point for one of two OLED options — more on that later. The sides of the chassis come equipped with two "full-function" USB-C ports and a headphone jack, and lifting the lid reveals an FHD camera with Windows Hello support to greet you.

On the specifications front, HP says it will support "up to" an Intel Core 7 processor, but the model currently on show is the only option available. The battery life numbers look rather impressive — up to 42 hours of local video playback via an unspecified-capacity battery — but I should point out that local video playback testing isn't exactly a benchmark that reflects real-world usage. HP mentions that the device is compatible with its 65W GaN mini charger, which I presume is included in the box. Beyond that, dual microphones and "Poly Studio-tuned" audio is everything we know about the device so far. If you feel like there's a lot that's still unclear, you're definitely not alone.

First of all, it's unclear which processor the US$700 version of the laptop will use, making it difficult to compare against Apple's A18 Pro. HP has also chosen not to disclose any storage or memory configuration details — not even an "up to" claim — which speaks volumes about how hard the PC market is struggling in the current RAM crunch. Even the device's biggest selling point comes with a rather significant caveat: HP spent most of its time hyping the 2.5K OLED display, but that version won't ship until March 2027. The model going on sale at Best Buy this month will come with a 2K OLED display, with brightness plummeting dramatically from 650 nits to just 300 nits.

There are still plenty of unanswered questions — along with some disappointing answers — but if HP has still managed to pique your interest, keep an eye out for more details to be released before it officially goes on sale.
